doc: Arrival-time and service-fact formatting rules. These are DOMAIN RULES, not wire shapes: no schema can generate them, so every platform hand-ports them and this corpus is the only thing that keeps the ports equal. Read the file, iterate `groups`, run each case, compare to `expect`. Conventions used throughout this directory: (1) JSON `null` means the language's absent value (TS `undefined`, Swift `nil`, Kotlin `null`) both in arguments and in `expect`; (2) `nowIso` is the clock reading, passed in because every rule here is pure; (3) arrivals are ISO-8601 with a fixed +08:00 offset, so lexical order is chronological; (4) `knownDefect: true` marks a case that records what the code does today and is AGREED to be wrong — see `note`. A defect row is not permission to diverge: fix it in every platform at once, in the same commit that edits the row. ETAs are approximations (ADR-008) — no rule here fabricates sub-minute precision.

etaView.doc: Signed seconds/minutes to arrival plus the two honesty flags. `minutes` is FLOORED, so it reads as whole minutes still remaining (countdown-board convention): 119 s is '1 min', not '2 min'. `isDue` is a symmetric +/-60 s window around the arrival, so a feed whose clock is a little behind still says 'Due' instead of flipping to a departed dash. Anything earlier than -60 s has departed.

cases.note: NAMED BOUNDARY ROW. One second under two minutes. Floor gives 1, so the label stays '1 min'. A port that rounds instead of floors shows '2 min' here and overstates the wait by a whole minute.
NAMED BOUNDARY ROW. Exactly two minutes — the first second at which the label reads '2 min'.
NAMED BOUNDARY ROW. One second past two minutes — still '2 min'. Together with the two rows above this pins the whole rounding rule with three cases.
Last second inside the 'Due' window.
The first second that shows a number rather than 'Due'.
60 s in the past is still 'Due', not departed — the tolerance band for feed clock skew. Note `minutes` is -1 because the floor of -1.0 is -1.
One second past the tolerance band. `minutes` is -2, not -1: flooring a negative goes away from zero (floor(-61/60) = -2). A port using integer truncation gets -1 here and will disagree.

formatRelative.doc: The rider-facing relative label. Under a minute it is a word, never a number. A departed bus is an em dash, never a negative number. Between 60 s and 119 s it is '1 min' (the value is clamped to at least 1, so the numeric slot never shows 0).

cases.note: NAMED BOUNDARY ROW, label side: 119 s reads '1 min'.
60 s..119 s all read '1 min'. The clamp exists so the badge never renders a bare '0'.
U+2014 EM DASH. Never a negative minute count.

etaLabelParts.doc: The same rule as formatRelative, split so a caller can render the number large and the unit small and pinned — only the digits move as the value changes. Three variants; the discriminator is `kind`.

cases.note: The departed variant has no text at all — the caller decides how to render an absence, so no platform invents a string here.

isStale.doc: Whether a reading is old enough to be shown as stale. Strictly greater than 90 000 ms since the feed generated it — the threshold second itself is still fresh. This is a data-quality signal, not an error.

cases.note: 90 000 ms exactly. The comparison is `>`, not `>=`.
Upstream clocks run slightly ahead sometimes. A future timestamp yields a negative age, which is never stale.

dedupeEtas.doc: Collapse rider-duplicate arrivals to one row per line, keeping the soonest. A rider thinks 'route number + direction', so the key is operator + route number + bound, parsed out of the canonical route id. `args.etas` carries only the three fields the rule reads (routeId, operator, arrivals); a port should fill the remaining required Eta fields with inert values. `expect` is the surviving routeIds, in output order (insertion order of first sighting).

cases.note: KMB indexes the same line under several service types. Two rows, one line; the 12:05 reading wins over the 12:09 one even though it arrived second in the list.
The KMB stop feed returns every direction of a route. Inbound and outbound must both survive — they are different journeys.
Route '10' exists for both KMB and Citybus. The operator is part of the key.

GMB route numbers repeat across regions, but a stop belongs to exactly one region, so two arrivals here sharing number+bound are always the same route (ADR-047). Collapsing them, keeping the sooner, is intended — not a bug.
The first sighting is kept provisionally even with an empty arrivals list; a later row with an actual time replaces it.

NAMED BOUNDARY ROW, and a REAL DEFECT (knownDefect). The dedupe key is built by joining three fields with '|' and nothing escapes a '|' inside a field. 'KMB:1|2:outbound:1' yields routeNo '1|2' + bound 'outbound'; 'KMB:1:2|outbound:1' yields routeNo '1' + bound '2|outbound'. Both flatten to the key 'KMB|1|2|outbound', so two distinct lines silently collapse and one arrival DISAPPEARS from the rider's list. The same unescaped-concatenation shape is what the favourites key `${memberStopId}|${routeId}` relies on (ADR-032, 'canonical ids carry colons, never a pipe'). Nothing validates that assumption today. `expect` records the broken behaviour so all platforms agree while it is broken; when the id parser enforces the grammar, `expect` becomes BOTH routeIds and every platform's suite goes red until it is ported.

formatFare.doc: A single HK$ figure for display. The upstream string is passed through verbatim — no float parsing, no re-rounding, so '6.70' stays '6.70'. A port must not reformat the number.

cases.note: Proves the pass-through: a port that parses to a number and reformats would print '$6.7'.
Recorded so no port 'helpfully' returns an empty string instead. Callers are expected to guard: fareRange/fareStages both skip blanks, so this is unreachable through them.

fareRange.doc: Cheapest/dearest across a set of boarding-stop fares. Compared NUMERICALLY but returned as the ORIGINAL upstream strings, so no float drift reaches the screen. Returns absent when nothing usable is present.

cases.note: The row that catches a string-sorting port: lexically '10.0' < '9.5', numerically it is the maximum.
JSON null is the absent value. The terminus carries no boarding fare, and some rows are blank or junk.

'6.70' and '6.7' are numerically equal; neither comparison is strict-greater/less, so the first-seen string is kept for both ends. This is what makes the flat-route collapse in formatFareRange predictable.

formatFareRange.doc: A sectional fare framed high-to-low, mirroring the route's own direction: dearest boarding at the origin, less from each later stage. The arrow is the same U+2192 used by the 'A -> B' route label, spaced on both sides. Collapses to one figure when the fare is flat.

cases.note: The separator is space + U+2192 RIGHTWARDS ARROW + space. Copy the character, do not substitute '->'.

Equality is string equality, so a range of '6.70'/'6.7' would NOT collapse. fareRange guarantees that cannot happen (see its first-of-two-equal-values row); this records the boundary in case something else builds the range.

fareStages.doc: Collapse a route's per-stop sectional fares (array index = seq - 1) into contiguous fare stages. `fromSeq`/`toSeq` are 1-based and inclusive. Consecutive stops with an EQUAL fare merge; a blank, absent or non-numeric fare breaks the run and is itself skipped.

cases.note: The last stop has no boarding fare, so it produces no stage at all.
The row that catches a port merging on fare equality alone. Stops 1 and 3 share a fare but stop 2 is blank, so they are TWO stages, not one spanning 1-3. Contiguity is part of the rule.
'6.70' and '6.7' are numerically equal but do not merge. Deliberate: the upstream figure is the source of truth and a change of printed form is a change of fare stage.

estimateChildFare.doc: A LABELLED ESTIMATE, not data: HK open data carries no fares by passenger type. Roughly half the adult fare, rounded to the nearest $0.1, always printed with one decimal. A bounded, deliberate exception to ADR-008 — the UI must always show it as an estimate. Rounding is half-away-from-zero on the tenths (not banker's rounding): a port using Kotlin's Math.rint or Python's round() will disagree on the .x5 cases.

cases.note: 3.35 -> '3.4'. Half-away-from-zero. This is the case that distinguishes rounding modes.
'17', not '17.0', would be wrong — the one-decimal form is part of the contract so a column of figures aligns.

A blank string coerces to 0 and yields '0.0' rather than absent, so a caller that forgets to guard prints a $0.0 child fare. Recorded rather than silently differing per platform; the caller is responsible for not passing a blank. See the note on estimateElderlyFare's matching row.

estimateElderlyFare.doc: A LABELLED ESTIMATE of the Government $2 Scheme fare for 65+/PwD riders, as amended 3 Apr 2026: $2 for adult fares up to $10, otherwise 20% of the adult fare — i.e. max($2, 20%), to one decimal. Requires an eligible/JoyYou Octopus, not cash. Changing the scheme means editing this group and re-porting.

cases.note: The scheme's hinge. 20% of $10 is exactly $2, so the floor and the percentage agree here and the result is $2.0 either way. A port that used a strict inequality on the wrong side still passes this row — the next two rows are what separate them.
A blank coerces to 0, and max($2, 0) is $2, so a missing fare silently becomes a confident '$2.0'. Same unguarded-input shape as estimateChildFare's blank row.

formatStopCount.doc: Route length as a stop count. The locale only selects the unit word; the figure is not localized.

cases.note: Reads '1 stops'. English has no plural rule here, so it is wrong. Chinese is unaffected (个站/個站 does not inflect). Recorded as a defect so a port does not quietly add an English-only plural and diverge; the fix belongs in the i18n layer with a plural-aware key, not in a per-platform special case.

formatJourney.doc: Whole-route journey time, always hedged. English prefixes a bare '~' with no space; Chinese uses 約/约 followed by a space. The asymmetry is deliberate typography, not an oversight.

formatHeadway.doc: Typical headway as a coarse range from the GTFS frequency bands — never a fabricated single figure. Collapses when min equals max. The separator is space + U+2013 EN DASH + space; the spacing is deliberate so the dash does not visually fuse with the digits.

cases.note: Separator is ' – ' (U+2013 with a space each side), NOT a hyphen and NOT unspaced.
Never 'every 12 – 12 min'.

formatServiceHours.doc: Daily service span on a 24h clock, locale-independent. Same spaced U+2013 EN DASH as formatHeadway. Note what this does NOT do: it performs no wrap normalization, so a past-midnight band value reaches the screen verbatim. Normalizing is the caller's job.

cases.note: '25:35' means 01:35 the next day in the GTFS frequency table (see FreqBand). This formatter prints it as-is, so a caller passing a raw band value shows a rider '25:35'. Recorded to pin responsibility: the wrap must be resolved before formatting, and any platform that 'fixes' it here diverges from the others.

classifyRemark.doc: A coarse class for an operator's free-text ETA remark, so the UI can style a timetable-derived arrival differently from a tracked one (ADR-008/036). The feeds carry prose, not codes, so this matches on text in both English and Chinese. English matching is case-insensitive. 'scheduled' is tested first and therefore WINS over 'lastBus' when a remark matches both. Anything unmatched is 'info' — never an error.

cases.note: Upstream shouts sometimes. The stem is 'schedul', so 'Scheduled'/'SCHEDULE'/'scheduling' all match.

NAMED BOUNDARY ROW (empty `en`, circular route). Upstream really ships a blank English remark on minor GMB circular services while the Chinese text is populated. The Chinese branch must carry the classification on its own; a port that reads only `en`, or that treats a blank `en` as a hard failure, gets 'info' here and styles a last-bus warning as ordinary information.

remark.zh-Hant: 大角咀(循環線) 尾班車已開出
remark.zh-Hans: 大角咀(循环线) 尾班车已开出

cases.note: The same blank-`en` shape for the other class. 未開出 ('not yet departed') is one of the scheduled markers.
Order of evaluation is part of the contract: a scheduled last bus is classed 'scheduled', because 'this is a timetable guess' is the more important caveat.
